Historical observations for this pairing come from measurements collected throughout the world’s oceans using a variety of methods. The earliest data were collected by inserting a thermometer into a water sample collected by lowering a bucket from a ship. Today, temperature measurements are collected more systematically from ships, as well as at stationary and drifting buoys. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has carefully reconstructed and filtered the data to correct for biases in the different collection techniques and to minimize the effects of sampling changes.

Model outputs are based on a set of 16 global climate models that reflect scientists’ current understanding of how greenhouse gases warm the atmosphere and how this heat moves between the atmosphere, water, and land. These same 16 models were used in the most recent National Climate Assessment. The modeled lines are smoother than the historical trends because the project team averaged 16 models together and also applied an 11-year smoothing filter, both of which smooth out year-to-year variability. However, the shaded bands do include year-to-year variability.

The graph shows annual anomalies, or the difference relative to the average temperature from 1971 to 2000.
